title: Benchmark Report (Latency/$) – Competitive FAQ and Objection Handling
author: Soojin Lee
body:
## Purpose
This page equips AEs/SEs/SDRs to respond to competitive pushback on Redwood Inference’s public **Latency per Dollar (latency/$)** benchmark report. It includes:
- Common competitor narratives (and why they come up)
- Approved rebuttals tied to our methodology
- Qualification questions to turn objections into discovery
- Escalation guidance (when to loop in Perf/Evals, SRE, or Legal)

**Audience:** Field (AEs/SEs), SDR/Inbound, CS (for renewals/expansion conversations).

**Important:** Use this to explain our methodology and what the metric means. Do **not** use it to claim “fastest/cheapest overall” beyond the specific workloads/regions and reported confidence language.

---

## Redwood framing (use verbatim where possible)
**What we measured:** production-representative workloads (chat + embeddings baseline), in specific regions, using a consistent harness and repeat runs.

**What latency/$ means:** “How much user-perceived latency you buy for a given spend at a defined throughput and workload shape.” It is a production economics metric that combines performance and cost.

**What the report is (and is not):**
- It is a reproducible comparison under defined conditions.
- It is not a promise that every customer workload will match the median result.
- It does not replace running a small reproduction on your own prompts, token distributions, and regions.

**Differentiation in one line:** Redwood is optimized for **serving** (latency, reliability, cost controls, and deployment flexibility) with a unified runtime and operational tooling across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.

---

## Claims guardrails (do/don’t)
### Do
- Emphasize **methodology transparency**, repeat runs, and variance language.
- Position results as **decision support** for engineering + procurement.
- Offer a **reproduction path** (small-scale run) for their workload.
- Say “in our measured setup” / “for the published workload and regions.”

### Don’t
- Don’t claim blanket superiority: “always fastest,” “best price,” “most accurate,” “beats everyone.”
- Don’t speculate on competitor internals (hardware, margins, caching policies) unless they are publicly documented.
- Don’t imply competitors are “lying” or “fake benchmarking.” Keep it factual: “different workloads/assumptions.”

**If pressed for absolutes:** redirect to “Let’s run your prompts + target region(s) under the same harness and compare.”

---

## Competitive pushback patterns (quick index)
1) “Latency/$ is a made-up metric.”
2) “You cherry-picked models / regions.”
3) “Your workload isn’t realistic (prompt sizes, concurrency).”
4) “You used caching/batching tricks that don’t apply.”
5) “Your price assumptions are wrong / discounts make this irrelevant.”
6) “You didn’t include reliability / tail latency / rate limits.”
7) “This is just a marketing benchmark; not reproducible.”
8) “We can do this with open source (vLLM/TGI) for cheaper.”
9) “Why not just use a hyperscaler managed endpoint?”
10) “These results won’t hold for Private / VPC / on-prem.”
11) “Region differences make the report misleading.”
12) “You didn’t include Model X / newest version.”

---

## FAQ with recommended responses (field-ready)

### 1) ‘Latency/$ is a made-up metric. Why should I care?’
**What they mean:** They want to shift the conversation back to a single axis they feel strong on (e.g., $/token or raw latency).

**Recommended response (short):**
Latency/$ is a unit economics metric for production inference. It combines the two things teams actually trade off in production—latency and spend—under a defined workload and throughput. We still report the underlying components (latency distributions, throughput, and cost), so you can validate it.

**Methodology tie-in:**
We compute latency/$ from measured latency percentiles and metered cost for the same run configuration. It’s not a black box; it’s derived from reported primitives.

**Turn it into discovery:**
- “What matters more for you right now: p95 latency, throughput under concurrency, or total monthly spend?”
- “What’s your user-facing SLO (p95) and expected QPS distribution?”

---

### 2) ‘You cherry-picked models/regions that make you look good.’
**Recommended response (short):**
We publish the coverage and inclusion criteria and we report results per-region. We picked a curated set based on customer demand and operational supportability, then ran the same harness across regions with repeat runs and variance checks.

**Methodology tie-in:**
- Coverage is defined ahead of time (model families + regions).
- Results are reported per-region; we don’t blend regions into a single number.
- Repeat runs + rerun policy reduce one-off wins from transient infra noise.

**Follow-ups:**
- “Which model(s) and regions are decision-critical for you?”
- “If the report doesn’t include your top model, we can run a targeted reproduction (or share roadmap for coverage).”

**If they ask to add their preferred model:**
Acknowledge. Capture model name, context length, expected TPS/QPS, and target regions. Route to Perf/Evals to validate inclusion and timing.

---

### 3) ‘Your workload isn’t realistic.’
**Recommended response (short):**
No benchmark represents every production workload. That’s why we publish the workload definition (prompt/response length distributions, concurrency, warmup) and encourage customers to reproduce with their own prompts. The goal is to be explicit and reproducible—not to claim universality.

**Methodology tie-in:**
- Workload definitions include chat + embeddings baselines.
- Concurrency and token distributions are fixed and documented.
- Warmup behavior and measurement windows are defined.

**Qualification questions:**
- “What’s your median input tokens and typical output tokens?”
- “Do you have bursty traffic or steady concurrency?”
- “Is streaming required? Tool/function calling? Structured outputs?”

---

### 4) ‘You used caching/batching tricks that don’t apply to real traffic.’
**Recommended response (short):**
We document caching and batching policies used in the benchmark. In real production, these are not “tricks”—they’re standard serving optimizations. The important part is that we apply policies consistently and measure end-to-end behavior under concurrency.

**Methodology tie-in:**
- Discloses caching policy (including warmup) and batching configuration.
- Same harness settings applied per model/region.

**Clarify applicability:**
- If their workload has low prompt reuse, caching benefits will be lower.
- If they have strict per-request latency caps, batching must be tuned—Redwood exposes those controls.

**Ask:**
- “Do you have repeated prefixes (system prompts, templates)?”
- “Is your traffic spiky enough that dynamic batching helps, or is latency extremely strict?”

---

### 5) ‘Your pricing assumptions are wrong; we get discounts.’
**Recommended response (short):**
Discounts vary by contract and volume, so we focus on a consistent pricing basis for comparability. If you share your expected volume and any existing GPU/commit structure, we can model the outcome for your case and run a controlled reproduction.

**Methodology tie-in:**
- Uses a single, documented pricing basis for the report.
- Keeps the metric comparable across regions and models.

**What to do next:**
- For enterprise: offer a side-by-side TCO model (Dedicated vs their current commit) using their committed rates.
- For PLG: point to public pricing and suggest a quick trial using their traffic.

---

### 6) ‘This ignores reliability / tail latency / rate limits.’
**Recommended response (short):**
We report latency distributions (including tail) and run with guardrails to avoid noisy runs. Reliability is a separate dimension; Redwood supports SLAs (Dedicated) and operational tooling (rollouts, fallbacks, observability). The report is a performance economics slice, not the full vendor scorecard.

**Methodology tie-in:**
- p50/p95 (and where applicable p99) are captured per run.
- Rerun rules handle anomalies and transient regional issues.

**Differentiate Redwood:**
- Dedicated capacity with predictable throughput and isolation.
- Built-in routing and fallback policies to preserve availability.
- Console observability to see token-level cost/latency per route/model.

**Ask:**
- “Is your pain mostly tail latency under load, or availability during bursts?”
- “Do you need capacity reservations or can you tolerate shared-host variability?”

---

### 7) ‘You can’t reproduce this; it’s just marketing.’
**Recommended response (short):**
We built the benchmark with a deterministic harness, standardized outputs, and repeat-run variance checks. We also provide guidance to reproduce a smaller-scale version against your workload. If you want, we’ll do a joint reproduction session in your target region.

**Methodology tie-in:**
- Benchmark harness runbook exists (environment setup, configs, sanity checks).
- Standardized output schema and deterministic table generation.
- Variance analysis and rerun triggers.

**Offer:**
- “Let’s run your prompts through the same harness and compare apples-to-apples.”

---

### 8) ‘We can do this with open source (vLLM/TGI) for cheaper.’
**Recommended response (short):**
You absolutely can self-host, and for some teams that’s the right choice. The question is the fully-loaded cost: engineering time, reliability, autoscaling, observability, upgrades, kernel/runtime tuning, security controls, and multi-region operations. Redwood productizes these so you get predictable latency/cost without building the serving platform.

**Differentiate Redwood (practical points):**
- Unified Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployment path (same API + tooling).
- Operational controls: rollouts, canaries, automatic fallback.
- Cost/perf levers with visibility: batching/caching/quantization profiles + token-level breakdowns.

**Discovery:**
- “Who would own 24/7 on-call, capacity planning, and model upgrades?”
- “Do you already have GPUs committed, or would you procure/operate them?”

---

### 9) ‘Why not just use a hyperscaler managed endpoint?’
**Recommended response (short):**
If hyperscaler endpoints meet your latency/cost targets, that’s a valid option. Redwood differentiates when teams need better serving economics, clearer operational tooling, or consistent behavior across hosted + dedicated + private. Our benchmark is built to make those economics legible.

**Differentiate Redwood:**
- Performance-tuned inference runtime and workload-aware batching/caching.
- Transparent per-route latency/cost observability.
- Deployment flexibility and consistent rollout controls.

**Ask:**
- “Are you optimizing for fastest integration, or for predictable latency and cost at scale?”
- “Do you need to run in multiple regions with consistent tooling?”

---

### 10) ‘These results won’t hold in VPC/on-prem (Private).’
**Recommended response (short):**
Private deployments introduce environment-specific factors (networking, instance types, cluster policies). The report is a baseline for our supported regions and configurations. The right approach for Private is a controlled proof using the same methodology with your constraints.

**Methodology tie-in:**
- Report results are explicitly scoped to published regions and runtime settings.

**Offer:**
- Propose a Private evaluation plan: target model(s), target hardware, success metrics (p95 latency, $/1M tokens, throughput), and a 1–2 week measurement window.

---

### 11) ‘Region-to-region differences make the report misleading.’
**Recommended response (short):**
That’s exactly why we publish results per-region. Region is a first-order variable (network distance, capacity availability, underlying fleet composition). We don’t hide that; we help you choose the right region and build routing/fallback policies to meet SLOs.

**Differentiate Redwood:**
- Smart routing policies and fallback across compatible variants/regions.
- Dedicated capacity options when predictability matters.

**Ask:**
- “Where are your users? Where must data reside?”
- “Do you need single-region residency, or can you fail over cross-region?”

---

### 12) ‘You didn’t include the newest model/version; this is outdated.’
**Recommended response (short):**
Model ecosystems move fast. We publish coverage and plan to refresh on a cadence. If a new model is important to your decision, we can run a targeted reproduction now and share results under the same harness.

**Operational follow-up:**
Capture: model name/version, context length, quantization constraints, and region(s). Route request to Perf/Evals for feasibility and timeline.

---

## “If they say X, say Y” (rapid-fire table)
Use this section for live calls.

- **X:** “Your benchmark is optimized for your platform.”
  **Y:** “We disclose the runtime settings and apply them consistently. The goal is to reflect production serving, not a micro-kernel contest. If you have a different traffic shape, let’s reproduce with your prompts.”

- **X:** “You’re hiding the raw data.”
  **Y:** “We publish a sanitized public table and the methodology. We don’t publish per-request logs because that can expose sensitive telemetry patterns. We can share additional aggregated breakdowns in an NDA setting.”

- **X:** “Your numbers are within noise.”
  **Y:** “We quantify run-to-run variance and rerun when thresholds are exceeded. If two options are within the confidence band, we’ll say so—and the decision typically comes down to reliability, operational controls, and deployment constraints.”

- **X:** “You picked favorable time windows.”
  **Y:** “Runs follow reserved capacity windows with guardrails to protect production SLOs and ensure consistency. We repeat runs and apply rerun rules when anomalies occur.”

- **X:** “This doesn’t include our security requirements.”
  **Y:** “Correct—this report is performance economics. For security/compliance, we have a separate FAQ covering data handling, logs, retention, and Private deployment controls.”

---

## How Redwood differentiates (anchor points for competitive conversations)
Use these when the buyer agrees the report is helpful but asks “why you?”

1) **Production economics, not just access to models**
- Latency/cost visibility by model/route
- Controls for batching/caching/quantization profiles
- Workload-aware tuning rather than one-size-fits-all

2) **Operational reliability and graceful degradation**
- Routing and fallback policies to maintain uptime
- Rollouts (canary/A-B) with safe rollback
- Dedicated capacity and predictable throughput options

3) **Unified platform across deployments**
- Same API and operational model for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private
- Supports data residency and regulated workloads without rewriting your app

4) **Benchmark credibility as a product habit**
- Deterministic harness + standardized outputs
- Repeat runs, variance analysis, and anomaly triage playbook
- Clear scoping and disclosure language

---

## Competitive traps to avoid
- Don’t let the conversation become “benchmark vs benchmark.” Bring it back to **their** workload, regions, and SLOs.
- Don’t fight on a single number. Offer to validate via reproduction and then discuss operational fit.
- Don’t hand-wave differences. If their workload differs materially (context length, tool calling, strict tail), say so and propose a targeted test.

---

## Escalation guidelines
Escalate when:
- Prospect requests an exception/clarification about methodology or wants additional unpublished cuts.
- Prospect challenges statistical validity or demands confidence intervals beyond what is published.
- Prospect alleges false advertising or asks for legally binding performance commitments.

Who to loop in:
- **Methodology/statistics:** Jonas Weber, Claire Dubois, Sana Farid
- **Runtime details / flags / tuning:** Markus Klein, Rina Kobayashi
- **Capacity/region behavior and incidents:** Sean Gallagher, Neha Kapoor
- **Claims/legal review:** Michael Grant

Suggested line while escalating:
“I want to make sure we answer precisely and stay consistent with the published methodology. Let me pull in our Perf/Evals lead to validate the details, and we’ll follow up with a written response.”

---

## Field checklist (before sending the report to a competitive account)
- Confirm target **model(s)** and **region(s)** are relevant to them.
- Ask for their expected **token distribution** (input/output), concurrency, and tail latency SLO.
- Offer a **reproduction plan** (small prompt set + 30–60 minutes of joint review).
- If procurement is involved, prepare a simple TCO framing (unit economics + operational cost) and avoid absolutist claims.

---

## Internal notes (for enablement owners)
This FAQ is intended to remain stable. If you hear new pushback patterns, add:
- the competitor claim as a direct quote
- which segment it appears in (startup vs enterprise; EU vs NA)
- the best-performing response (what moved the deal forward)

Owner: Soojin Lee (updates), with review by Markus Klein (technical accuracy) and Michael Grant (claims guardrails).
